sections.body:
This is a story about a small robot called Bit. He lives in a workshop with a bench, a toolbox and a charging post. He is the only robot there.

Bit has a plan. He has read about friendship in a book. He will go outside. He will find a child. He will say hello. The child will be so happy to meet him that they will be friends before sunset.

A good adventure has a shape. It has a beginning, a middle and an end. The beginning tells you who is going and why. The middle brings the surprise. The end gives you something worth keeping.

This adventure has that shape. At the beginning, Bit is full of a big simple plan. In the middle, the plan falls apart in the rain. At the end, Bit finds a friend he never planned for.

Read it slowly. Laugh where it is funny. Then tell the story to someone you trust.
examples: This story is about a small robot who wanted a friend.
A good adventure has a beginning, a middle and an end.
I can tell this story again tomorrow.
sections.heading: What this robot adventure is about

sections.body:
Bit's **sensor** is a small glass eye in the middle of his head. It lights up blue when Bit is happy and red when he is worried.

This morning it is blue. Bit has his plan.

He climbs down from the charging post, which is where he gets his **battery** filled. He pushes open the workshop door. He is going to find a friend.

The street outside is bright and loud. Children shout. Cars go past. A dog barks. Bit's sensor flashes red, then blue again, then red.

He tries the first thing in his plan. He walks up to a boy on a bicycle.

"Hello," says Bit. "Would you like to be my friend?"

The boy pedals faster. The bell on his bicycle goes ding, ding, ding.

Bit tries a girl with a skipping rope. She looks at him, then looks at her mother, and pulls her mother along by the sleeve.

Bit tries a man in a shop doorway.

"Would you like to be my friend?"

The man says, "No thank you," and goes inside.

By lunchtime, Bit's sensor has been red for a long time. Something is wrong with his plan. He knows how to ask the question. He does not know what people want to hear first.
examples: His sensor was blue when he was happy and red when he was worried.
He walked up to a boy on a bicycle and said hello.
The man said no thank you and went inside.
sections.heading: The beginning: the plan with a hole in it

sections.body:
The rain starts at two o'clock. Bit has no coat, because nobody told him robots need coats.

Water goes into his joints. It goes into the little motor of his left leg. His steps start to sound wrong. Squelch. Squelch.

Bit finds a bus shelter. He leans against the glass and watches the rain. His sensor is red. He does not know what to do next.

Then a small girl comes running into the shelter. She is soaked. She has a paper crown on her head that has gone soft and droopy.

"It fell in the water," she says. "My paper crown."

She is not crying, exactly. She is more disappointed than sad. A crown is a serious thing to lose.

Bit looks at the crown. He looks at his own hands. His hands are flat metal plates. They are very good at lifting heavy things. They are not good at making paper.

"Wait here," says Bit.

He goes out into the rain. He walks to the workshop. He finds the toolbox. He finds a sheet of shiny silver paper, a pen, and a small pair of scissors.

Then he sits down in the shelter and works. He cuts a crown. He draws stars on it with the pen. He gives it to her.

She holds it up. It is not much of a crown. It is the best crown anybody has made for her in a long time.
examples: His steps started to sound wrong. Squelch, squelch.
A small girl ran into the shelter with a wet paper crown.
It was not much of a crown, and it was the best crown anybody had made for her.
sections.heading: The middle: the rain that ruined the plan

sections.body:
The girl puts the crown on. She looks at Bit with the crown crooked on her head.

"Thank you," she says. "What is your name?"

"Bit," says Bit.

"I am Linh. Do you want to come to my house? It is close. We can draw the crown."

Bit's sensor goes blue. But then it goes red again, because something is wrong.

"I cannot leave," says Bit. "I have to plug in at the workshop."

Linh thinks about this. She looks at the rain. Then she looks at Bit.

"Then I will come to the workshop," she says.

So Bit walks home in the rain, and Linh walks beside him, holding the umbrella over Bit's head instead of over her own. His sensor stays blue the whole way.

And on the bench in the workshop there is something waiting. It is a small box, and inside the box is another robot. It is old, and dented, and it has one arm.

"This is my grandmother's robot," says Linh. "She says it needs somebody to look after it. But she is not here any more."

Bit looks at the old robot. Then he looks at the door.

The old robot has a **button** on its chest. Bit presses it, just once, the way you would knock on a door.

"Hello," says Bit. "I am Bit. Would you like to be my friend?"

And this time, somebody says yes.
examples: She held the umbrella over Bit's head instead of over her own.
On the bench there was an old robot with one arm.
sections.heading: The surprise: the friend who was not a child

sections.body:
These are the words you will meet in this story. Learn them here, and you can use them in your own sentences.

A **sensor** is a small sense organ on a robot. It tells the robot what is around it, or how it feels.

A **battery** is the store of energy that makes a robot move. When it runs low, the robot has to plug in.

A **button** is a small switch you press to make something happen. Pressing a robot's button can wake it up or start it.

Charging means filling a battery with energy. A **charging post** is the place where a robot goes to be filled.

A **workshop** is the room where a robot is built and repaired. It is full of tools, and it smells of metal and oil.
examples: A sensor tells a robot what is around it.
A robot with a low battery has to plug in.
The workshop is where robots are built.

sections.body:
What did Bit learn? He learned that his plan had a hole in it. He had thought friendship was a question you ask. It is not. It is something you do for somebody.

He also learned that a friend is not always the kind of friend you expect. Bit walked the whole street looking for a child. The friend who said yes was a dented old robot with one arm, and the friend who helped him was a girl with a paper crown.

Here is how to tell this adventure to someone. Keep the order, and the surprise will land in the right place.

Start with who is going and why. Tell the hard part in the middle. Save the surprise for last. Then say the small lesson in one short sentence.

The lesson of this adventure is this: do something useful first. A friend is easier to make after you have helped.
examples: The story starts with a robot leaving his workshop.
The surprise comes at the very end.
Do something useful first, and then a friend is easier to make.
sections.heading: The small lesson, and how to tell the story
steps: Start with the character: Bit leaves the workshop with his big plan.
Tell the middle: nobody says yes, and then the rain ruins everything.
Tell the surprise: the paper crown, the girl, and the old robot in the box.
End with the lesson: do something useful first, then a friend is easier to make.

item.summary: A small robot called Bit leaves the workshop to find a friend, and nothing goes the way it planned. Follow him through the street, the rain and the park at night. After reading, you can retell the adventure, use five new robot words in your own sentences, and explain how Bit finally made a friend.
item.title: The Robot Who Wanted a Friend
